brief.outcome: Choose and launch a price and package that lift average revenue per account by 25% within the year, with monthly churn staying at or under 2.5% and every existing customer keeping their price for at least 12 months.

ambition.goal_beyond: Pricing that follows the value architecture firms get, so revenue per account keeps growing as a firm grows, without losing the trust of today's customers.
rungs: Pick a higher per-user price for new customers by looking at the $40 to $70 competitor range.
Find what architecture firms value and will pay, choose what to charge for and the tiers, test the new price on new customers only, and plan the move for existing customers after their 12 months.
Do rung 2, then make pricing a standing review: a quarterly price test and a tracked gap between list and realised price, with churn watched against the 2.5% limit.
ambition.judge: Stripe invoices and subscriptions: revenue per account for new customers against the old price, and monthly churn for new and protected customers, plus what customers themselves say in the survey.

brief.deliverable: A decided price and package, a bounded test of it on new customers launched with the founders' approval, a draft plan for existing customers after their 12 months, and an honest readout against the 25% target.

answers.question: What business and how many customers?
answers.answer: Project management tool for architecture firms, 340 customers.

answers.question: What is the price now?
answers.answer: One plan at $29 per user per month; the average account has 8 users.

answers.question: How do competitors compare?
answers.answer: Competitors charge $40 to $70. Sales say firms rarely push back on price.

answers.question: What is the goal?
answers.answer: Average revenue per account up 25% within the year, without monthly churn going above 2.5% (now 1.8%, Stripe).

answers.question: What must not change?
answers.answer: Existing customers keep their price for at least 12 months.

answers.question: What can your AI reach?
answers.answer: Stripe read access and a customer list export; we can email customers for a survey.

answers.question: Where should data live and who decides?
answers.answer: In a Google Sheet. The founders decide together.

research.approach: Practitioners do not set a price from competitor lists or from how little sales hear about price. They rebuild revenue per account and seats from billing records, decide what the product should charge for (the value metric) and how to package it, then ask buyers what they would pay with a structured price survey, and read competitor prices against what each includes. Because sales silence is weak evidence, they also check lost deals. A new price goes to new customers first, as a bounded test with a floor and a rollback rule, while existing customers keep their price on the old billing price. They also size the target first: when existing customers are protected, the in-year lift can only come from new customers and from users and tiers customers choose to add.

sources.title: Your pricing is (probably) broken (Kyle Poyar, Growth Unhinged)
sources.note: Flat fees, feature tiers and per-seat pricing each have known flaws and fixes: premium editions and add-ons, a clear purpose per tier, minimum users or a lighter seat. Only the free part of a paid post was read.

sources.title: Calculating average revenue per user in Billing (Stripe Support)
sources.note: Stripe's ARPU is total MRR divided by active subscribers; the page does not say whether discounts are counted. No date on the page; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: Change the price of existing subscriptions (Stripe Docs)
sources.note: A price change must replace the subscription item or a second price is added; updating a price resets quantity to 1 unless it is passed again; schedules can manage a change at period end. Matters for the later move of existing customers. No date on the page; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: Van Westendorp price sensitivity (Conveo Docs)
sources.note: Four ordered prices (too cheap, cheap, expensive, too expensive); the intersections are method-defined, not a proven profit-maximising price; low samples and unclear framing make the range unstable. No date on the page; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: Pricing research webinar: Van Westendorp and Gabor-Granger (QuestionPro)
sources.note: Seen in search results, not opened in full: about 100 completes as a floor for either method, more per segment when comparing. Vendor guidance and sources disagree on sample size, so treat as a rough floor. No date on the page; accessed 2026-11-03.

steps.name: Rebuild revenue per account, seats and churn from Stripe records
steps.why: Every pricing claim starts from what accounts really pay, how many users they have and how they change.

steps.name: Read competitor prices against what each includes
steps.why: A list price of $40 to $70 means little without knowing the plan, limits and extras behind it.

steps.name: Check lost deals and discounts, not just the absence of pushback
steps.why: Sales hearing little about price does not show the price is too low.

steps.name: Ask customers what they value and what they would pay
steps.why: A structured price survey gives a range and shows what scales with value, within known limits.

steps.name: Size the 25% target against the 12-month price protection
steps.why: With existing prices fixed, new customers and added users or tiers must carry the whole lift.

steps.name: Choose what to charge for and the tiers
steps.why: The value metric and packaging matter more than the exact number.

steps.name: Test the new price on new customers only, with a floor and a rollback rule
steps.why: It protects existing customers and shows the effect on win rate, revenue per account and early churn.

steps.name: Plan how existing customers move after 12 months
steps.why: The move needs notice, a safe Stripe method and its own churn watch; drafted now, used later.

steps.name: Raise existing customers' price now
steps.why: The quickest way to lift revenue per account.

pitfalls.text: Taking 'firms rarely push back' as proof of underpricing; it may reflect who sales talk to and what they quote.
Treating Van Westendorp intersections as the profit-maximising price, or reading them off a small or narrow sample.
Surveying existing customers in a way that signals a rise, breaking the 12-month promise in spirit.
Changing the price in Stripe by adding a second price instead of replacing the item, or losing the user count because quantity resets to 1.
Using a different revenue-per-account definition for the target than for the baseline, such as counting discounts one way and not the other.
Keeping a flat per-user fee that prices small firms out and gives large firms no reason to pay more, when add-ons or tiers could fix it.

stages.name: Pin down the problem
stages.goal: Turn the owner's words into a measured problem, a target, limits and the data we can reach. Writes BRIEF.md.

stages.name: Rebuild revenue per account and seats from Stripe
stages.goal: Load raw subscription and invoice history into the Google Sheet and rebuild revenue per account, the spread of users per account, seat growth over time, discounts and monthly churn.

checks.name: Rebuilt revenue per account is within 3% of $232 ($29 x 8 users), or the gap is explained by discounts, annual plans or user counts
The number of paying accounts matches the customer list's 340 within 2%
The revenue-per-account definition (recurring revenue per active account, discounts in or out) is written down and used for baseline and target

stages.name: Read competitor prices and lost deals
stages.goal: Record each named competitor's plans, limits and extras from its public page with the date, and summarise won and lost deals, discounts and stated reasons.

checks.name: Every competitor price has a link and the date it was seen
Each price is shown with what is included, and plans with different scope are not compared directly
Deal findings state the number of deals behind them; fewer than 20 deals is marked low-confidence

stages.name: Ask customers what they value and would pay
stages.goal: Draft a short survey with the four Van Westendorp price questions, a ranked list of what matters, and size and role questions; the owner reviews and sends it, and valid answers go into the Sheet.

checks.name: No question or email names a planned price or suggests existing customers' prices will change
Only complete answers in strict ascending order are used, each exclusion has a recorded reason, and results with fewer than 100 valid completes are labelled directional only
Answers are tagged by firm size from the customer list so segments can be compared

stages.name: Check the numbers can be trusted
stages.goal: Check billing, customer list, survey and competitor data agree before reasoning from them, and that the churn figure uses Stripe's definition.

checks.name: Rebuilt monthly churn is within 0.2 points of the reported 1.8%, or the definition difference is stated
At least 95% of survey responses match a customer in the list, and the unmatched are listed
Ends with CHECKED, LIMITED or UNRELIABLE and what that means for the diagnosis

stages.name: Test whether the price is too low and what it can reach
stages.goal: Test the hypotheses: stated willingness to pay, competitor scope, lost deals, what scales with value, seat growth, and what the 25% needs given the 12-month price protection. Keep competing explanations.

checks.name: States the new-customer revenue per account, and the number of new customers, needed to lift the all-account average by 25% with 340 accounts held at current prices; says plainly if that is out of reach in 12 months
Every hypothesis is SUPPORTED, REFUTED or UNKNOWN with numbers
A price range is reported with its sample size and the curve intersections, and is not presented as the profit-maximising price
Each main finding names a competing explanation

stages.name: Rank price and package options
stages.goal: Turn findings into ranked options: new-customer price, what to charge for, tiers and add-ons, each with a revenue model that includes churn and win rate, and the month-13 path for existing customers.

checks.name: Every option cites the finding it rests on
Every option shows revenue per account, churn and win-rate assumptions in a low, middle and high case, with the churn that would breach 2.5%
No option changes an existing customer's price, users or plan within 12 months
Every option has a price floor from cost to serve, or says that cost data is missing

stages.name: Founders choose
stages.goal: The founders pick an option. Ask for the reason when the top option is passed over, and record it.

checks.name: Chosen and passed-over options are in decisions.jsonl
A reason is recorded wherever the top option was passed over

stages.name: Build the new-customer test and the month-13 plan
stages.goal: Write the test design (who sees the new price, how long, floor, rollback rule), the pricing page and package wording for the owner to apply, and a draft plan with notice wording for existing customers after 12 months. Nothing is sent.

outputs.name: Month-13 plan for existing customers (draft, not for sending)

checks.name: The test states the primary measure (revenue per new account and win rate), the guardrail (monthly churn at or under 2.5%) and the minimum of 30 new customers per price before a verdict
The steps change only the price shown to new customers and name how to confirm existing subscriptions are untouched
Any later Stripe change replaces the subscription item and passes the user count, per Stripe's guidance

stages.name: Show the new price to new customers
stages.goal: Register the test, then the owner applies the approved price to new sign-ups and we read back that no existing subscription changed.

checks.name: The test is in experiments.jsonl with its floor, guardrail and rollback rule before the price goes live
A before and after comparison of all existing subscriptions shows zero price or quantity changes
The live page and the new Stripe price were read back and match the approved wording

stages.name: Read results against the limits
stages.goal: Read revenue per new account, win rate and monthly churn for new and protected customers against the 25% target and the 2.5% limit, using Stripe records. Read-only.

checks.name: Revenue and churn figures are rebuilt from Stripe records, not from our sheet, using the same definition as the baseline
A verdict is given only with at least 30 new customers per price, otherwise INCONCLUSIVE
Monthly churn for new and for protected customers is each checked against 2.5%, and a breach triggers the rollback rule
Average revenue per account is reported against $290 with the mix of new and existing accounts, and a miss is reported as a miss

stages.name: Keep what we learned
stages.goal: Close the test, save rules with their scope, and plan the move for existing customers and the next round.

checks.name: The test is closed in experiments.jsonl with its verdict

hypotheses.statement: Architecture firms would accept a price well above $29 per user.
hypotheses.test: Van Westendorp curves from valid survey answers, overall and by firm size, with the sample size shown.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The optimal price point is $35 or more and the upper end of the acceptable range is $39 or more, on at least 100 valid completes.
hypotheses.refute_if: The optimal price point is $31 or less, or the upper end of the acceptable range is under $35.

hypotheses.statement: The lack of price pushback means the price is too low.
hypotheses.test: Share of lost deals that cite price, discount frequency and win rate, from the last 12 months of deal notes.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Price is cited in fewer than 10% of lost deals, discounts are rare, and win rate is above the team's own target.
hypotheses.refute_if: Price is cited in 25% or more of lost deals, or discounts are common.

hypotheses.statement: Competitors at $40 to $70 sell a comparable scope.
hypotheses.test: Compare plans, limits and included modules for each named competitor.
hypotheses.confirm_if: At least three competitors with comparable scope list at $40 or more per user.
hypotheses.refute_if: The higher-priced plans include materially more modules or limits.

hypotheses.statement: Charging per user is not how value scales for architecture firms.
hypotheses.test: Survey ranking of what firms value, and whether firm size or project volume tracks revenue better than user count.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Another measure ranks first for at least 40% of respondents, or tracks stated value more closely than user count.
hypotheses.refute_if: Users rank first or tie, and user count tracks value.

hypotheses.statement: Revenue per account can rise through users and tiers that customers choose to add.
hypotheses.test: Quantity changes per account over the last 12 months from Stripe.
hypotheses.confirm_if: At least 20% of accounts added users in the last 12 months and average users per account rose at least 5%.
hypotheses.refute_if: Fewer than 10% of accounts changed quantity.

hypotheses.statement: With 340 accounts held at current prices, new customers alone cannot lift the all-account average by 25% in 12 months.
hypotheses.test: Solve for the new-customer revenue per account needed, given the real number of new customers expected in 12 months.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The required new-customer revenue per account is more than 1.8 times the current $232 (about $418).
hypotheses.refute_if: The required figure is 1.3 times the current figure ($302) or less.

hypotheses.statement: A higher new-customer price pushes early churn over 2.5% a month.
hypotheses.test: Monthly churn for new customers on the new price against the old price, in the live test.
hypotheses.confirm_if: New-price customers churn at 1 point or more above the old-price group, or above 2.5%.
hypotheses.refute_if: The two groups are within 0.5 points and below 2.5%.

hypotheses.statement: Larger firms would pay materially more per user than smaller firms, so tiers by size fit.
hypotheses.test: Compare survey price ranges across firm-size bands.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The upper end of the acceptable range for the top size band is at least 25% above that for the smallest, with at least 30 answers in each.
hypotheses.refute_if: The ranges are within 10% of each other.

dropped.reason: Existing customers keep their price for at least 12 months, which the owner set as a limit; their move is drafted for month 13 only.

measurement.window: Weekly checks on new sign-ups; first verdict when at least 30 new customers per price have been seen; churn for new customers read monthly; the 25% target read at month 12 with the account mix shown.
measurement.min_volume: At least 30 new customers on each price before a verdict, and at least 100 valid survey completes before the survey range is treated as more than directional.
measurement.stop_rule: Roll back to the old new-customer price if monthly churn for new-price customers passes 2.5% for two months in a row, or win rate falls by more than a third from its recent level; otherwise run the full window.
